newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ATHLETICS-LONG DISTANCE MARKS AT RISK IN BRUSSELS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-LONG DISTANCE MARKS AT RISK IN BRUSSELS.

text.p: Three long distance world records are under threat at the Brussels Grand Prix athletics meeting on Friday, organiser Wilfried Meert said on Monday.
Meert said Kenya's 5,000 metres world champion Daniel Komen had asked for a 5,000 metres race to be added to the programme.
"You can well guess why," Meert told a news conference.
Komen will bring his own pacesetters and would be "super motivated", Meert said.

He said Komen felt very frustrated after last week's 5,000 metres race in Zurich where Ethiopia's Halie Gebrselassie destroyed his own world record with a time of 12:41.86 ahead of Komen, who "had served as pacesetter to Gebrselassie for several kilometres", Meert said.
World 10,000 metres champion Gebrselassie, who also holds the world record for that event -- 26:31.32 set in Oslo last month -- will instead run the 3,000 metres in Brussels.

"He's now got the 5,000 and 10,000 record. He doesn't have the 3,000 record. Don't have me saying he'll certainly beat that record too because it's very strong. But he certainly wants to run very fast," Meert said.

He said he had been informed by Gebrselassie's Dutch manager Jos Hermens that the Ethiopean was not troubled by a slight injury sustained in a car crash last Thursday and had resumed training in Addis Ababa.
The 10,000 metres race will feature a three-man battle between Moroccan Salah Hissou and Kenyans Paul Tergat and Paul Koech for the second year in a row.
All three broke the 27 minute barrier in Brussels last year with Hissou snatching the world 10,000 metres record from -- Gebrselassie.
"They're all three back now...Gebrselassie has put the bar very high, (his record) is an incredible time but both Tergat and Hissou have said they'll do whatever they can to attack it," Meert said.
But he added he had given up taking out insurance against world record attempts.

"It's bizarre but for many years we were insured but missed out on the records, often by a whisker. It's not like we're superstitious or anything but the past two years we had no insurance and twice we had world records," Meert said.
Brussels offers a $25,000 bonus for world records.
The Brussels meeting, which is forecast to take place in fine weather conditions, will field 24 world champions, 14 Olympic champions and nine world record holders.
Like last year, the crowd of 39,000 has been promised an extra incentive to cheer on the athletes -- a free glass of beer.
